title: The Best Reason for Challenging Others to Defend What They Believe
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note reframes why good leaders push back on others' opinions: not primarily to expose flaws or win an argument, but to develop people's capacity for deeper self-reflection and critical thinking. It offers a list of specific, curiosity-driven questions designed to gently surface the assumptions underlying someone's view without triggering defensiveness. The piece argues that well-crafted challenging questions open conversations rather than shutting them down, and positions this kind of Socratic questioning as a core teaching function of exceptional leadership.
points: Challenging others' viewpoints is framed primarily as a talent-development tool, not a way to win arguments.
A list of curiosity-driven questions is offered to surface the assumptions underlying someone's opinion.
Well-crafted challenging questions are said to open dialogue rather than triggering defensiveness.
This kind of Socratic questioning moves people 'off script' from their automatic, rehearsed responses.
The piece concludes that exceptional leaders are, fundamentally, teachers who build critical thinking in others.
quotes: the best leaders do this primarily to stretch and develop how others think.
They accomplish this by crafting questions that invite team members to engage in self-exploration about the assumptions underlying their opinions.
The best questions gently force others to look at the assumptions underlying their views and examine the thinking and feelings just below the smooth surface.
Carefully worded questions have the potential to open up conversations rather than shutting them down.

Instead, they understand the power of a curious but challenging question to promote open dialogue, engender the exploration of ideas, and to teach people how to think more critically. Exceptional leaders are always teachers.
